# When the Edge Decays {#sec-edge-decay}

Part III began with a paper that found an edge in a casino and ended with the casinos changing the
rules. That sequence is the subject of this chapter, generalised: **an edge is not a property you
acquire. It is a state of the world that a finite number of other participants have not yet noticed,
and it is subject to erosion from the moment it exists.**

The practical consequence is that the useful question is not "do I have an edge" but "how fast is
this edge decaying, and what will replace it". This chapter treats the answers as an ongoing
obligation rather than a one-time discovery.

## Four mechanisms of erosion

They operate on different timescales. Separating them clarifies what can be managed. Four mechanisms.

**Imitation.** Fastest. The edge becomes visible, someone copies it, and the copies compete away the
advantage. This is the fastest mechanism and the one most under the discoverer's influence.

**Capacity.** Slower. The edge itself shrinks as capital is applied, because the trading moves the prices
that created the opportunity. This is the mechanism of Chapter 23, and it operates even if nobody
copies anything.

**Rule change.** Outside control. The institution that made the edge possible alters its behaviour: exchanges change
fee structures, regulators change rules, counterparties change terms. This is the casino mechanism,
and it is outside the practitioner's control.

**Discovery of the underlying regularity.** Slowest. A statistical relationship that was genuinely unknown
becomes known, and the knowing removes it. This is the slowest mechanism and the most fundamental,
because it applies to any edge whose existence depends on others being unaware.

| Mechanism | Timescale | Under your control? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Imitation | Quarters | Partly: by staying small |
| Capacity | Quarters to years | Partly: by capping size |
| Rule change | Years, and abruptly | No |
| Discovery of the regularity | Years to decades | No |

**The table's second column is the reason a decay-aware sizing rule beats a decay-aware forecast.**
Two of the four mechanisms cannot be influenced at all, and the other two can only be slowed. What
can be done is to size for the possibility rather than to predict the timing.

## What makes an edge durable

The erosion rate depends on what the edge is made of, and three sources behave differently.

**Structural frictions persist longest.** Longest of all. A fee schedule, a regulatory constraint, a settlement
process, a tax treatment: these are created by institutions and persist until the institutions
change. An edge that exists because of a rule lasts about as long as the rule.

**Capacity limits protect their own beneficiaries.** Partly shielded. An edge whose exploitation is limited by market
depth is partly shielded, because the limit that constrains you also constrains imitators. This is
why small-capacity strategies survive longer than large-capacity ones, and why the most durable edges
are usually the least scalable.

**Behavioural regularities decay with awareness.** Shortest life. An edge that exists because participants
systematically misprice a risk disappears as the mispricing becomes known. This class has the
shortest life, and it is the class that most quantitative work is aimed at.

**The practical implication is a preference ordering for new work: an edge with a documented
structural source is worth more than an edge with a good statistical record**, because the first
carries information about its own persistence and the second does not.

## The maintenance obligation

If an edge decays, then finding one is not a project with an end date. Three obligations follow.

**Re-estimation on a schedule.** Not continuously, because continuous re-estimation is noisy, but at
intervals fixed in advance. The interval should be shorter than the expected decay time and longer
than the noise in the estimate, which is a narrow window in practice.

**Monitoring for the mechanisms rather than the returns.** Watching returns is the slowest possible
way to detect decay, because a shrinking edge is hidden inside the noise for years. Watching the
mechanisms is faster: is the trade getting more crowded, are fills getting worse, is the spread
narrowing, is a rule under discussion.

**Planning the exit before it is needed.** Chapter 16's pre-committed exit applies with particular
force here, because the alternative is to keep running a decaying strategy while deciding, month
after month, that the evidence is not yet conclusive. **That is exactly the position the sampling
arithmetic of Chapter 24 predicts, and it is where most decayed edges continue to be traded.**

## The paradox of a successful edge

There is a structural feature here worth stating plainly. It follows. because it
explains a pattern in the industry that otherwise looks like foolishness.

**Success brings capital. Capital accelerates decay. Therefore the more successful an edge is, the
faster it destroys itself.**

The practitioner who scales a working strategy is behaving rationally in the short run and
self-destructively in the long run, and the two horizons are the same horizon — which means the
decision cannot be resolved by better analysis. It is a genuine trade-off between present return and
the survival of the thing generating it.

Chapter 23 supplied the resolution, such as it is: **prefer the smaller size that persists to the
larger size that removes its own premise.** The preference is not modesty and not risk aversion. It
is the arithmetic of an asset whose expected life shortens when you use it.

## Three practical responses

**Prefer edges whose protection is structural.** Structural first. The preference ordering above, applied when choosing
what to work on rather than when deciding how much to stake.

**Size for the current edge, not the historical one.** Current, not historical. A shrinking edge means the historical average
overstates what is available now, and a sizing rule based on the historical estimate overbets in
exactly the way Chapter 21 described.

**Treat the exit as part of the strategy.** Write it down. A strategy without a stated stopping condition is a
strategy that will be run past its useful life, because the decision to stop is made by the same
person with the same incentives at the moment of maximum ambiguity. **Writing the stopping condition
in advance converts a monthly judgement into a rule.**

## Grading it

**That edges decay is grade II.** It survives changes of market, era, and strategy type, and the
mechanisms are documented sufficiently that the burden of proof sits with anyone claiming permanent
advantage.

**The relative durability of the four sources is grade II as well**, and weaker: the ordering is
argued from the mechanisms rather than measured, and a systematic study of edge lifetimes across
sources would be the appropriate test.

**The prescriptions are grade III**, as with every practical rule in this part.

## Claim and tool

The claim: an edge is a decaying asset, and the decay is partly caused by the use of the asset.

The tool: the four mechanisms and their timescales, the durability ordering by source, and the three
obligations — re-estimate on a schedule, monitor the mechanism rather than the returns, and write the
exit before it is needed.

## Boundary conditions

The chapter assumes that the edge's sources can be identified, which is the same requirement Chapter
18 imposed and which many claimed edges fail.

It assumes that the decay is gradual rather than abrupt. Where rule changes are the dominant
mechanism, decay can be instantaneous, and no monitoring interval is short enough.

And it says nothing about how to find the replacement edge, which is a research problem rather than a
sizing problem.

## Monitoring decay without watching returns

Watching returns is the slowest way to detect decay. This section lists faster indicators, each tied to
one of the four mechanisms.

**Crowding. Fast.** Count the participants who appear to be doing the same thing. New entrants, new
fund launches in the same niche, and increased public discussion are all observable without any
estimate.

**Fill quality. Faster still.** Compare realised slippage against the model used to justify the
strategy. A deterioration in fills is the earliest sign that the trade is being competed for, and it
appears in the data before returns move.

**Spread compression. Direct.** Where the edge consists of capturing a spread, the spread's narrowing
is the edge's disappearance, measured directly rather than inferred.

**Rule discussion. Institutional.** Where the edge depends on a fee schedule, a settlement rule or a
regulatory constraint, the relevant indicator is the state of the discussion about it. Ignoring that
is the most common way to be surprised by an abrupt decay.

**Cost drift. Slow but reliable.** Compare the all-in cost per unit of position now against the cost
when the strategy was designed. Costs drift upward as capacity is consumed.

**Why these are better.** Each is a leading indicator of the mechanism rather than a lagging
consequence of the outcome. Each requires no forecast. And each can be observed by someone who is not
running the strategy.

**How to use them.** Fix a monitoring interval in advance, record the indicators alongside the returns,
and treat a deterioration in two or more as a trigger for re-estimation. Do not wait for the returns
to confirm it.

## Replacing a decayed edge

The chapter has argued that an edge is a decaying asset. The obvious question is what to do when one
decays, and the honest answer is that the capability to answer it has to be built before it is needed.

**Three preparations, all of which cost something now.**

**Keep a pipeline.** A research process that produces candidate edges continuously, at a rate above
the observed decay rate. The requirement is arithmetic: if edges last three years on average, a
pipeline that produces one per year will eventually run dry.

**Keep the machinery.** Execution, risk, and settlement infrastructure outlives any particular edge. A
firm that can deploy capital cheaply can move between edges; one that cannot is committed to whichever
edge it happens to hold.

**Keep the record.** Documented mechanisms and measured decay rates for past edges make the next
capacity judgement better. This is the only part of the chapter that compounds.

**What cannot be prepared.**

**The replacement itself.** No process guarantees finding a new edge, and treating research as a
production line with a known yield is a category error.

**The timing.** Decay arrives when it arrives. The pre-committed exit from the ledger is what converts
an unplanned event into a scheduled review.

**A judgement about the capability.** Some practitioners are better at finding edges and others at
running them at scale. A firm that concentrates the second capability and neglects the first will have
excellent execution and nothing to execute.

**The uncomfortable arithmetic.** A pipeline that produces edges at the historical rate, run through a
process with the historical decay, is a business with a known half-life. **Planning for that half-life
is more useful than assuming the last edge will persist.**

## The decay rate as a planning parameter

If edges decay, the decay rate enters every decision about how much to invest in finding them, and it is
usually left implicit. Making it explicit changes the arithmetic.

**The quantity.** The expected time from deployment of an edge to the point where its return falls below
the cost of running it.

**Three typical values, by source, from the durability ordering.** A behavioural regularity exploited by
many participants: months to a few years. A structural friction tied to an institutional rule: the life
of the rule. A capacity-limited edge in a small market: as long as the market's structure persists, which
can be decades.

**What the rate determines.**

**The research budget.** A firm with edges lasting three years needs a pipeline producing at least one
edge every three years, and realistically more, since not every candidate works.

**The sizing decision.** A shorter-lived edge justifies a larger stake and an earlier exit, because the
cost of being early is smaller than the cost of being late. **This cuts against the sizing rules, and the
resolution is that both effects are real: the discount is about estimation error and the decay rate is
about the horizon.**

**The organisational structure.** A firm whose edges last three years cannot amortise fixed costs over a
decade, which puts a floor on scale that a firm with a structural edge does not face.

**Why the rate is rarely stated.** Because estimating it requires observing edges die, and the
survivors' histories are what get recorded. **An organisation that keeps a register of retired edges,
with their lifetimes and the mechanism of their death, is in a position to make this estimate and almost
no organisation does.**

## The end of an edge, described

Decay is usually discussed as a trend. Its ending is usually abrupt, and the two phases require different
responses.

**The gradual phase.** The edge's return falls, gradually at first and then visibly. **The leading indicators
of the previous section move before the returns do, which is the reason to monitor them.**

**The abrupt phase.** A rule change, a competitor's entry at scale, a structural shift in the market. **The
edge's return does not decline; it disappears within days or weeks.**

**The distinction matters because the two phases have different tell-tale signals.** The gradual phase is
detectable from fills, spreads and crowding. The abrupt phase is detectable from **the discussion about the
rule**, which is why that indicator is on the list and why it is the one most often dismissed as noise.

**Three preparations for the abrupt phase.**

**A drawn-down plan.** What happens to the capital, the team and the infrastructure when a strategy stops.
**A plan written while the edge works is a document; one written during the ending is a crisis.**

**Revenue concentration limits.** A firm whose income depends on one edge has an abrupt ending risk that is a
governance issue rather than a research issue.

**A register of retired edges.** Their lifetimes, their mechanisms of death, and the indicators that preceded
the end. **This is the only source of evidence about the abrupt phase, and almost no organisation keeps it.**

**What cannot be prepared.** The timing. **An edge ends when its conditions change, not when its participants
are ready, and the pre-committed exit is what converts the event into a scheduled response rather than a
surprise.**

**Why the ending deserves its own section.** Because the gradual phase is what practitioners plan for and the
abrupt phase is what happens, and the difference between a managed ending and an unmanaged one is entirely a
matter of what was written down beforehand.

## The decay estimate as a research output

The decay rate is described as a planning parameter. It is also a research result, and treating it as one
changes how a research programme is organised.

**What a decay estimate consists of. Three items.**

**The edge's source.** Structural friction, behavioural regularity, or capacity limit. **Which determines the
expected lifetime more than any measurement.**

**The observed lifetime of comparable edges.** From a register of retired strategies, where one exists.

**The mechanism of death, where known.** Imitation, capacity, rule change, or discovery.

**Why the estimate belongs in the research output. Two reasons.**

**It determines the research budget.** A programme producing edges that last three years needs a pipeline
producing at least one every three years, and realistically more. **The arithmetic is simple and it is rarely
performed.**

**It determines the sizing.** A shorter-lived edge justifies a larger stake and an earlier exit, because being
early is cheaper than being late.

**What the estimate cannot be. Precise.** A lifetime estimate from a small register of retired edges carries
wide uncertainty, and reporting it with a decimal place would misrepresent it. **An order of magnitude is the
honest form.**

**Three ways to improve it cheaply.**

**Record every retired edge with its dates and mechanism.** Which is administrative work with a long payoff.

**Classify by source rather than by strategy.** Which aggregates across strategies and yields more observations
per category.

**Review the register annually.** Which is when the aggregate becomes visible.

**Why the output is worth requiring.** Because an edge without a lifetime estimate is a position without a
horizon, and the horizon determines both the stake and the exit. **Two questions at the point of discovery, and
the answers are the research output.**

## The decay register

The chapter argues that a register of retired edges is the only source of decay estimates. This section
describes the register, because an instrument described only in principle is one that nobody keeps.

**Four fields per retired edge.**

**One. The dates of deployment and retirement.** Which give the lifetime, the register's primary output.

**Two. The mechanism of death.** Imitation, capacity, rule change, or discovery. **Which is the field that
makes the register more than a list of lifetimes.**

**Three. The indicators observed before the end.** Which of the four leading indicators moved, and when
relative to the retirement decision.

**Four. What was done about it.** Whether the exit was pre-committed, forced, or late. **The most informative
field and the one that is hardest to record honestly.**

**What the register produces. Two outputs.**

**A decay rate by mechanism.** Which is more useful than an average rate, because the mechanisms have
different lifetimes.

**A calibration of the leading indicators.** Whether the indicators moved before the returns, and by how much
lead time.

**What keeping it costs. Ten minutes per retirement.** Which is the reason it is rarely kept and the reason
its information is unavailable.

**How to start with no history. Two moves.**

**Record the current edges at deployment, with their sources and dates.** Which begins the register with live
entries rather than none.

**Reconstruct the last few retirements from documents.** Which is imperfect and provides the order of
magnitude the estimates require.

**Why the register is worth the ten minutes.** Because the decay rate determines the research budget, the
stake size and the exit timing, and it is otherwise unobtainable. **Four fields, ten minutes, and it is the
only instrument in the book whose value grows with the number of entries.**

## The decay argument in four claims

The chapter is long and its argument has four steps, each of which can be checked separately.

**Claim one. Edges decay.** The mechanism is competition for a favourable state, and the mechanisms are
imitation, capacity, rule change, and discovery. **Grade II: robust across markets and periods.**

**Claim two. The decay rate depends on the edge's source.** Structural frictions tied to rules last as long as
the rules; behavioural regularities last until they are noticed; capacity-limited edges last as long as the
market's structure. **Grade II and weaker, because the ordering is argued from mechanisms rather than
measured.**

**Claim three. The decay is partly caused by using the edge.** Success attracts capital, capital consumes
capacity, and the consuming is what ends the edge. **Which is the chapter's most consequential claim and the
one that makes the sizing decision a trade rather than an optimisation.**

**Claim four. Decay can be monitored through mechanisms rather than returns.** Four leading indicators:
crowding, fill quality, spread compression, and rule discussion. **Which is the practical claim, and it is
checkable against a register of retired edges.**

**What each claim's grade implies. One instruction.** Rely on claim one, treat claim two as an expectation, act
on claim three by sizing smaller than the optimum, and use claim four as a monitoring specification with the
expectation that it is roughly right. **Four claims, four dispositions, which is what the book's grade
vocabulary is for.**

**What would falsify the set. One observation.** A structural edge with a documented mechanism whose return
did not decline as capital was applied over a long period. **Such cases exist in the material and the chapter
notes that the most durable edges are the least scalable, which is a partial accommodation rather than a
refutation.**

**Why the four claims are worth separating.** Because the chapter's practical recommendations depend on claims
three and four, and claims one and two are what make them plausible. **A reader who accepts the first two and
doubts the last two has a coherent position, and stating the claims separately makes it available.**

## The decay argument and the research programme

The chapter's four claims imply an organisational design, and the design is worth stating because it differs
from the one most firms have.

**What the claims require. Three things.**

**A pipeline whose output rate exceeds the decay rate.** Which follows from claim one and claim two: if edges
last a certain time, the programme must produce replacements at least as fast.

**Sizing below the optimum.** Which follows from claim three: using the edge consumes it, so the growth-optimal
stake is not the longevity-optimal one.

**A decay register.** Which follows from claim four: the leading indicators need calibration, and calibration
needs retired edges.

**What the design looks like. Three features.**

**Research capacity sized to the decay rate rather than to the current book of edges.** Which is a smaller
number for the short-lived sources and a larger one for the long-lived.

**A stated standing rule about capacity.** Which is the pre-commitment that prevents the successful edge from
being scaled until it dies.

**An annual review of the register.** Which is when the aggregate becomes visible and when the durability
ordering can be tested against the firm's own record.

**What the design costs. One thing.** Foregone return in the periods when a large stake would have worked.
**Which is the same cost the discount imposes and is borne in the same way: visibly, in comparison with a peer
who did not.**

**What the design cannot supply. The replacement edges.** Which is a research problem and not a structural one.
**The design keeps the firm in a position to use replacements; it does not produce them.**

**Why the organisational implication belongs with the decay claims.** Because the claims make a specific demand
— a pipeline rate, a sizing rule and a register — and a chapter about decay that stopped at the description
would leave the demand implicit. **Three features, each following from one of the claims, and the register is
the one that makes the others measurable.**

## The decay rate and three planning decisions

The decay rate is a planning parameter. Three decisions depend on it, and each uses it differently.

**The research budget. Directly.** A programme producing edges that last three years needs at least one per
three years, and realistically more. **Which is a rate calculation and the one decision where the estimate is
used as an input rather than a caution.**

**The stake. Inversely.** A shorter-lived edge justifies a larger stake and an earlier exit, because being early
is cheaper than being late. **Which cuts against the estimation discount, and the resolution is that the two
effects are about different things: the discount concerns how well the edge is known, the decay rate concerns how
long it will be there.**

**The exit. As a date.** A pre-committed exit for a strategy with an estimated three-year life is a review at
eighteen months, not a rule triggered by returns. **Which is the operational form of the decay estimate.**

**What the three share. One property.** Each uses an order of magnitude rather than a precise number. **Which is
fortunate, because the estimate cannot be precise: it comes from a small register of retired edges.**

**What the three do not include. The replacement.** Which is a research problem rather than a planning one. **The
three decisions keep the firm in a position to use replacements; none produces them.**

**How to use a decay estimate honestly. One statement.** "Edges from this source have lasted between two and five
years in our record, so the review is set at eighteen months and the research pipeline is sized for one
deployment every two years." **Which is a sentence a manager can act on and which contains its own uncertainty.**

**Why the three decisions are worth stating together.** Because the decay rate is usually invoked as a general
caution and the three above are where it enters arithmetic. **A rate used as an input, an inverse relation to
size, and a date — three uses, one estimate.**

## The decay claims and three kinds of counterexample

The chapter's claims are stated with their refutation conditions. Three kinds of counterexample would be
informative, and each tests a different claim.

**A structural edge whose return did not decline under large scale.** Which would test the durability ordering
and, and above all, the claim that use causes decay. **Such cases exist and the chapter notes that the most
durable edges are the least scalable, which is a partial accommodation rather than a refutation.**

**An edge that decayed without any of the four mechanisms operating.** Which would test the mechanisms'
completeness. **Finding one would mean a fifth mechanism, and the first place to look is a change in the
population of participants rather than in any of the four.**

**A leading indicator that moved without subsequent decay.** Which would test the monitoring specification. **The
indicator list is argued from mechanism rather than calibrated, so a false positive is as informative as a false
negative.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** Each is a claim whose test requires a register rather than an
experiment. **Which is why the register is the chapter's practical recommendation and why the absence of such
registers is the reason none of the three has been tested.**

**Which counterexample would be most damaging. The first.** Because claim three — that use causes decay — is the
one that makes the sizing decision a trade rather than an optimisation. **A durable, scalable structural edge
would reduce the claim to a description of most edges rather than a property of all.**

**How a firm could test the three. One register.** Lifetimes, mechanisms of death, indicators observed before the
end, and what was done. **Four fields per retired edge, ten minutes, and the aggregate answers the three
questions after a few years.**

**Why the refutation conditions are worth listing again here.** Because the chapter's claims are the ones the
book's sizing advice rests on, and a reader who accepts them without knowing their tests has accepted them on
authority. **Three counterexamples, one register, and the tests are within a firm's reach.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The chapter is an argument from mechanism, not from measurement. I located no systematic study of
edge lifetimes by source type, and the durability ordering is therefore a reasoned expectation rather
than a finding.

The claim that the most durable edges are the least scalable is drawn from the capacity mechanism
rather than from data, and a reader who knows a counterexample should treat it as one.
